 tightens cyber oversight of non-bank payment ﬁrms ajinkya kawale Mumbai, 5 November At a time when vulnerabilities driven by artiﬁcial intelligence are posing challenges to pay- ment systems globally, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Thursday issued a consoli- dated cybersecurity rulebook for all non-bank payment system operators (PSOs). The rulebook also brings annual system audits and third-party automated teller machine (ATM) switch providers under its ambit. The revised Master Direc- tions on Cyber Resilience and Digital Payment Security Con- trols apply to entities including the National Payments Corpor- ation of India, card networks, payment aggregators, prepaid payment instrument issuers and white-label ATM operators (WLAOs), among others. The directions take effect immediately for large and medium PSOs. Small PSOs have until April 1, 2028, to comply. PSOs are required to “obtain the source code of all critical applications procured from third-party vendors”. Where this is not possible, an escrow arrangement must be in place “to ensure continu- ity of services”, according to the notiﬁcation. If a PSO does not own the code, it must obtain a certiﬁ- cate from the developer stating that the application is “free of vulnerabilities, malwares, and any covert channels in the code”. A fresh certiﬁcate is required after every change. PSOs must also have “a mechanism to apply them immediately” for critical patches released to address known or reported attacks. Under the new system audit norms, PSOs must submit an annual audit report within two months of the close of their ﬁnan- cial year. For entities follow- ing an April- March ﬁnancial year, this means a deadline of June 1. To avoid conﬂicts of interest, neither the auditor nor its sister con- cerns must have provided any services to the entity during the preceding two ﬁnancial years. Auditors must also report any deviation from the process ﬂow submitted by the entity to the RBI while seeking authorisation. Open observations must be resolved within a “maximum three months”. WLAOs that use shared ATM switch services must con- tractually require their service providers to comply with cybersecurity controls on an ongoing basis and provide the RBI with access “for on-site/off- site supervision”. These con- trols include disabling remote connections from external machines to the switch net- work and blocking “potential backdoor connections”. PSOs must also ensure that unregulated entities in their eco- system, such as payment gateways and vendors, comply with the directions, “subject to mutual agreement”. The rulebook retains the requirements to report cyber incidents — including cyberat- tacks, outages of critical sys- tems or infrastructure, internal fraud, and settlement delays — to the RBI within six hours of detection. It also retains the requirement to impose a mini- mum 12-hour cooling-off period after a customer changes their registered mobile number or email address. The RBI said the consolida- tion would “provide a single reference point for the entities”. Six earlier circulars, the oldest dating back to 2009, have been repealed. large and medium payment operators must comply immediately, while small payment system operators have until april 1, 2028
